# Go — explicit behaviour, small examples

Each block below is a **separate complete program**. Put one block in main.go and run with Go.

## 1. Pointers change a caller's value

~~~go
package main
import "fmt"
func double(n *int) { *n *= 2 }
func main() {
    x := 3
    double(&x)
    fmt.Println(x) // 6
}
~~~

The expression &x takes the address of x; *n dereferences it. Go still passes the pointer value as an argument by value.

## 2. Slices can share a backing array

~~~go
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
    a := []int{1, 2}
    b := a
    b[0] = 9
    fmt.Println(a) // [9 2]
}
~~~

A slice copies a descriptor, not necessarily its underlying elements. Append can allocate a different backing array; sharing after append is not guaranteed.

## 3. Interfaces are implemented implicitly

~~~go
package main
import "fmt"
type Greeter interface { Greet() string }
type Person struct{}
func (Person) Greet() string { return "hello" }
func say(g Greeter) { fmt.Println(g.Greet()) }
func main() { say(Person{}) } // hello
~~~

No implements clause is necessary. The compiler checks the method set. A method using a pointer receiver changes which concrete types satisfy the interface.

## 4. Goroutines communicate through channels

~~~go
package main
import "fmt"
func main() {
    done := make(chan int)
    go func() { done <- 42 }()
    fmt.Println(<-done) // 42
}
~~~

The unbuffered receive waits for the send. Goroutine scheduling order is NOT fixed by source-code order.

$$
\operatorname{send}(x)\prec\operatorname{receive}(x)
$$

**Symbols:** send(x) and receive(x) are matching channel communication operations; the ordering symbol expresses their communication dependency, not an ordering of every operation in every goroutine.

**Substitute numbers:** x=42. The reader can start first, but it cannot finish receiving the value 42 before the corresponding send.

## 5. Errors are explicit return values

~~~go
package main
import ("fmt"; "strconv")
func double(s string) (int, error) {
    n, err := strconv.Atoi(s)
    if err != nil { return 0, err }
    return n * 2, nil
}
func main() { fmt.Println(double("21")) } // 42 <nil>
~~~

A conversion can fail, so the caller needs both the result and error. For cancellation, pass context.Context to operations that can honour cancellation.

**Sources:** [A Tour of Go](https://go.dev/tour/welcome/1), [Effective Go](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go), [Go Memory Model](https://go.dev/ref/mem).
